newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas deputy ministers work towards trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Americas deputy ministers work towards trade deal.

text.p: Deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the Americas made some progress on Tuesday on hammering out a deal on a region-wide free trade zone but remained short of resolving the main differences, officials said.
Jose Artur Denot Medeiros, Brazil's envoy to the Latin American Aladi group, said there was a lack of consensus over "fundamental" issues, namely what shape formal negotiations should take.
"Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed," he said.

The deputy ministers were in the industrial city of Belo Horizonte to draw up a declaration for their political bosses to sign on Friday at the end of the third ministerial meeting of Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) signatory countries.

Launched at the Miami summit in 1994, the FTAA envisioned the setting up of a free trade area of one billion potential consumers by the year 2005 that would rival the economic muscle of the European Union.

Trade and foreign ministers, due to gather in Belo Horizonte May 15-16 after the deputy ministers conclude their talks, were supposed to determine the timetable and nature of formal free trade negotiations.
But progress has been blocked by disagreement between Brazil, speaking for Mercosur, and Washington.

Brazil is keen to strengthen Mercosur. And, faced with a ballooning trade gap, it is uneasy over the prospect of taking on further tariff-reduction obligations that would allow the entry of more imports. It urged "caution and prudence" in progress towards the FTAA.

Brazil also sought assurances from Washington that free trade will apply to all sectors, including agriculture, and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso sent a clear message on Monday to Washington that it would have to give as well as take.
The United States, on the other hand, is determined to push through free trade as fast as possible.
Medeiros said negotiations had got stuck on paragraphs four and five of the ministerial declaration.
The first refers to a consensus on launching formal talks after a presidential FTAA summit in Santiago, Chile next March. The latter concerns the order and content of the talks.
But Medeiros stressed there was "no confrontation" and that there was a "desire by all" to reach agreement.
Parallel to the official talks in Belo Horizonte, hundreds of businessmen from across the region were pouring into the city of two million people to hold a forum starting Wednesday.
Labour leaders from across the Americas began meeting Monday and were expected to present Tuesday to the deputy ministers a list of their demands and suggestions.

One of the decisions the Belo Horizonte meeting is expected to make is whether to allow the labour movement greater involvement in the negotiation process by allowing it to also hold parallel forums similar to the businessmen.
